title: Ang 947–956: Ramkali ki Var M3
tomorrow: why would anyone sing 'all ties are false' at a wedding?

segments.voice: Last time, ang 938: the yogis asked Guru Nanak who his guru was, and he answered, the Word. Today, a song with a borrowed tune.

Movie trailers do it all the time: an old song everybody knows, slowed down, with a new meaning poured into it. Ang 947 does it too. Above the third Guru's ballad in Ramkali sits a note for the singers: sing this to the tune of the ballad of Jodha and Vira of Purbani. Two warriors, tradition says, whose fight the bards sang in village squares. So picture the crowd. They already know the tune. They lean in for the battle. What they get is a different fight.
screen: `AN OLD SONG, A NEW MEANING.` → `THE TUNE OF JODHA AND VIRA.` → `A DIFFERENT FIGHT.`

segments.voice: A var is a ballad, the old form for heroes: stanzas called pauris, sung with drive. In the Granth's vars, saloks, short verses, sit before the pauris, and Ramkali ki Var, by Guru Amar Das, follows that pattern. The tune note is the clue. The bards' version was about warriors and a fight that ended in blood. The Guru's version keeps the beat and moves the battlefield inside: the self against ego, the mind wandering off and coming home to the Name. The hero isn't someone on horseback. It's the gurmukh, the one who turns toward the Guru. So why borrow the tune? The Granth doesn't explain; it simply gives the instruction. But one reading is easy to see. People already carried that rhythm in their bodies. It stirred them. The Guru didn't ask them to drop it. He gave the same beat a new story to carry, and a familiar sound became a way in. There's a kind of mercy in that. No one has to learn a strange new melody to hear an old truth. They only have to listen to the words this time. Same drum, different war. That's the ballad.
screen: `A VAR: A BALLAD FOR HEROES.` · `SALOKS, THEN PAURIS.` · `THE BATTLEFIELD MOVES INSIDE.` · `A FAMILIAR BEAT, A WAY IN.` · then, large: `THE BALLAD.`

segments.voice: If you can stand, walk slowly for a minute to a steady beat in your head, left, right, like a ballad's pulse. Then sit for the rest of the time and let the beat keep going in the breath, nowhere to march to. If you'd like, read the tune note at the top of ang 947, or the pauri on ang 948, first.
Ang 947. Where Ramkali ki Var begins, the third Guru's ballad, sung to the tune of an old warriors' song.
The ballad: an old tune, a new battlefield, and the fight is inside. Onward, gently.
